concept.name: Speed
concept.definition: Speed is a third-order sensitivity of an option's value: the rate of change of gamma with respect to the underlying price, i.e., the third derivative of value with respect to the underlying price. It measures how quickly a position's convexity changes as the underlying moves.
concept.intuition: If delta is your speedometer and gamma your accelerator, speed is how fast the accelerator itself stiffens as the stock moves — it warns you that your gamma hedge will go stale.
concept.mechanics: Speed = d(gamma)/dS = d3V/dS3. It is relevant to gamma-hedged books because a large move changes not just delta but gamma, so the re-hedge quantities computed at current prices are wrong after the move; speed is largest for near-ATM options and changes sign across the strike.
concept.failure_modes: Third-order Greeks are extremely model- and input-sensitive: small errors in implied volatility produce large speed errors, so hedge prescriptions based on speed are indicative at best. In discontinuous markets the smooth-derivative framing breaks down entirely.
concept.misconceptions: Speed is not how fast an option's price moves — it measures the curvature of gamma across price, a book-management quantity with no intuitive P&L meaning for simple positions.
concept.example: A gamma-hedged book re-hedged assuming gamma 0.06 finds gamma has fallen to 0.04 after a $2 rally because speed was negative at that strike; the hedge quantities were therefore over-stated.
